ligustrum-obtusifolium.summary: Border privet is a spreading, many-stemmed shrub often planted as a hedge. Small oval leaves grow in opposite pairs, and narrow clusters of white flowers are followed by black fruits that can persist into the colder months. Its branches spread broadly, giving an untrimmed plant a loose, layered shape. The leaves may turn reddish-purple in autumn, with some retained in mild conditions. This Asian shrub has escaped cultivation in Connecticut, where it can establish in lightly managed areas.

sources.label: Cornell Turfgrass and Landscape Weed ID: Border privet

parthenocissus-tricuspidata.summary: Boston ivy is a deciduous woody vine from eastern Asia, familiar on walls and other vertical surfaces. Branched tendrils end in adhesive pads that anchor the stems firmly. Mature leaves are usually broad and three-lobed, turning red or burgundy in autumn; young growth can carry three separate leaflets. Small blue-black fruits, often on red stalks, attract birds. Although commonly cultivated, it also grows outside gardens in disturbed places and on rocky ledges in parts of New England.

saponaria-officinalis.summary: Bouncingbet, also called soapwort, is an upright perennial with smooth stems and opposite, lance-shaped leaves marked by several strong veins. Clusters of pale pink or white flowers bloom at the stem tips. Each flower usually has five slightly notched petals emerging from a long, narrow green or reddish tube; double-flowered garden forms also occur. Originally from Eurasia, it was widely cultivated. Its soapwort name recalls the saponins in the leaves, which were formerly used to make a washing liquid.

cydalima-perspectalis.summary: Box tree moth is an Asian moth whose caterpillars feed on boxwood. The larvae are green with black heads and contrasting dark and pale lengthwise stripes. They tie foliage with silk, leaving webbing, droppings and chewed leaves inside the shrub. Heavy feeding can strip the leaves and damage bark. Adults usually have white wings bordered broadly in dark brown, though a darker form also occurs. Hidden caterpillars among dense foliage make careful inspection of the plant's interior useful.

sources.label: CFIA: Box tree moth fact sheet

monarthropalpus-flavus.summary: Boxwood leafminer is a tiny fly whose young live and feed inside boxwood leaves. Infested leaves develop yellowish spots and swollen, blisterlike mines that later turn brown; heavy attacks can thin a shrub as damaged leaves fall early. The orange to reddish adults resemble small gnats and appear around boxwoods in spring. Several larvae may share one leaf. Because the insects are concealed between the leaf surfaces, checking the leaves themselves is more useful than looking only for flying adults.

centaurium-pulchellum.summary: Branched centaury is a small annual with delicate pink flowers above pairs of oval leaves. It often branches near the base and may stay only a few inches tall. Unlike some other centauries, it does not form a lasting rosette of leaves at ground level. Its tiny flowers have short stalks and a narrow tube that opens into spreading lobes. Native across parts of Europe, Asia and northern Africa, it occurs in North American fields and other disturbed ground as an introduced plant.

schizoporella-errata.summary: Branching bryozoan is a colony of tiny marine animals that builds a hard crust over rocks, shells and harbor structures. Older portions can become thick, dark brown or purplish, while growing edges are paler; some colonies develop folded sheets or hollow branches. Its animals collect suspended food with fine tentacles. Originally described from Naples, it is associated with warm coastal waters. Similar bryozoans have often been confused with it, so older reports from distant coastlines need careful checking.

sources.label: Tompsett, Porter & Taylor (2009), Taxonomy of Schizoporella unicornis and S. errata

begonia-hirtella.summary: Brazilian begonia is a small, soft-stemmed tropical plant with green leaves covered in fine hairs. It can flower while still only a few centimeters tall, producing small white blossoms above the foliage. Its papery brown fruits hold numerous dustlike seeds. The species is native to Jamaica and parts of tropical South America and favors moist tropical settings. It is also found outside that range; Singapore records it as a casual nonnative plant rather than assigning it a broad invasive status.

sources.label: Kew Plants of the World Online: Begonia hirtella

jasminum-fluminense.summary: Brazilian jasmine is a woody, evergreen climber with opposite leaves divided into three leaflets. Its white, tubular flowers open into narrow spreading lobes and have a noticeable fragrance. Despite its common name, the species comes from Africa and the Arabian Peninsula. Introduced as an ornamental, it has escaped cultivation in southern Florida, where it can climb into forest canopies and cover other vegetation. Birds and mammals carry its seeds, helping it spread away from planted vines.

sources.label: UF/IFAS Center for Aquatic and Invasive Plants: Jasminum fluminense
Kew: Jasminum fluminense, including Flora of Somalia account

alternanthera-brasiliana.summary: Brazilian joyweed is a long-lived herb or small shrub often grown for its purple or reddish foliage. Leaves grow in opposite pairs, and small whitish flowers gather into rounded or slightly elongated heads on slender stalks. Shaded plants may be much greener than plants in sun. Native from Mexico through tropical America, it has been planted elsewhere as an ornamental. Stems can root where they touch the ground, and discarded cuttings can help it spread beyond gardens.

sources.label: UF/IFAS: Alternanthera brasiliana weed risk assessment

solanum-seaforthianum.summary: Brazilian nightshade is a sprawling perennial shrub or climber grown for loose clusters of mauve-blue, star-shaped flowers. Its leaves are deeply divided, and the flowers are followed by small, bright red berries. The stems lack prickles, a useful feature when comparing it with other nightshades. It has escaped ornamental plantings into moist sites in parts of Australia. In Florida, current guidance varies by region, with central and southern areas advised to manage plantings to prevent escape.

schinus-terebinthifolia.summary: Brazilian Peppertree is an evergreen shrub or small tree with dense branches, glossy compound leaves and clusters of small red fruits. The leaves have several leaflets along a central stalk, which may be narrowly winged. Native to South America, it was widely planted as an ornamental and now forms dense thickets in parts of Florida and Hawaii. Birds help disperse its single-seeded fruits. It grows in many disturbed and natural habitats, including relatively dry ground within otherwise wet landscapes.

sources.label: US Forest Service FEIS: Brazilian pepper

schinus-terebinthifolia-var-raddianus.summary: Brazilian peppertree appears in this catalog under an older variety name. Kew now treats the corrected form, Schinus terebinthifolia var. raddiana, as a synonym of the typical variety. The broader species is an evergreen shrub or small tree with compound leaves and red fruits, but those features do not distinguish this historical variety. Keeping the naming history visible helps connect older records with current references without implying that this entry represents a separately identifiable plant.

verbena-brasiliensis.summary: Brazilian vervain is a tall, rough-haired herb with branching stems and slender spikes of tiny bluish-purple flowers. Opposite, toothed leaves sit directly on the angular stems. Native to South America, it grows in fields, roadsides, damp grassland and stream margins where introduced, including North Carolina. It is easily confused with other tall verbenas. The small flower size and the bracts projecting among the flowers are more useful clues than its overall silhouette alone.

eichhornia-paniculata.summary: Brazilian water hyacinth is an aquatic herb that holds its leaves and branching flower clusters above the water. Its broad leaves have heart-shaped bases and long, slender stalks that are not swollen. A study in northeastern Brazil described upright plants about 25–60 centimeters tall with many flowers in each cluster. Current botanical references place it in Pontederia as Pontederia paniculata. It is a separate species from the familiar floating water hyacinth, so that plant's growth habits and impacts should not be assumed here.

egeria-densa.summary: Brazilian Waterweed is a submerged freshwater plant with long, branching stems and dense rings of bright green leaves. Rooted near the bottom, it grows upward and often concentrates its foliage close to the surface. White flowers rise to the water surface during warmer months. Native to South America, it became familiar through ponds and aquariums. In invaded Washington waters, thick growth can crowd other aquatic plants, slow water movement and interfere with recreation.

sources.label: Washington Invasive Species Council: Brazilian elodea

poranopsis-paniculata.summary: Bridal bouquet is a vigorous climbing vine with broad, heart-shaped leaves and large sprays of tiny white flowers. The undersides of its leaves are covered in pale, silvery hairs, giving foliage a two-tone appearance. Native from the Indian subcontinent to Myanmar, it has been cultivated in other warm regions. Hawaiian specimens document vines spreading across fences, shrubs and trees, sometimes reaching well into the canopy. The small flowers may have a faint sweet fragrance.

sources.label: Bishop Museum Plants of Hawai‘i: Poranopsis paniculata

campanula-cervicaria.summary: Bristly bellflower is a rough-haired wildflower with pale blue to lilac bells packed into rounded clusters. Its lower leaves are narrow, and the upright stem is thick and angular. Plants often begin as a leafy rosette before flowering in a later season. It grows around woodland edges, open woods and other partly open habitats in Europe. Its status deserves local attention: conservation work in Bavaria aims to support remaining populations, showing why a catalog listing alone cannot establish that a plant is unwanted.

sources.label: Bavarian Environment Agency: Campanula cervicaria conservation
Conservatoire botanique de Lorraine: Campanula cervicaria

cynosurus-echinatus.summary: Bristly dogstail grass is an annual grass with a dense, egg-shaped flower head covered in long, stiff bristles. Its narrow leaves are flat, and its upright stems may grow alone or in small tufts. Each head contains a mixture of fertile and sterile flower units, which contributes to its distinctive bristly outline. In British Columbia it occurs in disturbed ground, dry forest edges and thin-soiled Garry oak habitats, where managing seed production can help protect sensitive native vegetation.

sources.label: Garry Oak Ecosystems Recovery Team: Cynosurus echinatus
Flora of New Zealand: Cynosurus echinatus

leontodon-hispidus.summary: Bristly hawkbit is a dandelion-like herb whose leaves form a rosette close to the ground. Flower stalks rise above it with yellow flower heads, while the leaves vary from lightly toothed to deeply divided. Many plants carry forked or branching hairs, although hairiness varies among forms. A familiar grassland plant in parts of Europe and the Alps, it is also recorded as an introduced plant in New England fields, lawns and roadsides. Mature fruits help distinguish it from similar hawkbits.

sources.label: FAO: Site-specific grasses and herbs, Leontodon hispidus

persicaria-longiseta.summary: Bristly Lady's Thumb is a low, often sprawling annual with slender spikes of tiny pink flowers. Its smooth stems bear alternate leaves, sometimes marked with a faint dark blotch. A papery sheath circles each leaf base, with conspicuously long bristles along its upper edge. Native to Asia, the species is introduced in much of eastern North America. At Fontenelle Forest in Nebraska it is common along trails, where its loose growth and small flower spikes can be easy to overlook.

sources.label: Fontenelle Forest Nature Search: Bristly lady's thumb

helminthotheca-echioides.summary: Bristly oxtongue is a coarse herb with yellow, dandelion-like flower heads and conspicuously rough leaves. Many of its hooked hairs arise from small raised bumps, giving the plant a prickly appearance. Beneath each flower head, several broad outer bracts surround a narrower inner set. It grows in fields, gardens, roadsides and other disturbed ground. Native around the Mediterranean region, it has been introduced elsewhere, including North America, and older references often call it Picris echioides.

sources.label: Kew: Helminthotheca echioides, Flora of Iraq

najas-minor.summary: Brittle Waternymph is a submerged freshwater plant with narrow, curved leaves and teeth visible along their edges. Leaves grow in pairs, though crowded shoots may look whorled. Its flowers and seeds are tiny and sit near the leaf bases. Native to parts of Europe, Africa and Asia, it has spread in North America through seeds and fragments. Some invaded waters develop dense growth, but effects vary: Wisconsin reports that nuisance-level growth has not been observed there.

galeopsis-tetrahit.summary: Brittlestem hempnettle is an annual in the mint family with square, bristly stems and opposite, coarsely toothed leaves. Clusters of tubular pink, purple or white flowers sit where the upper leaves meet the stem. Each blossom has an arched upper lip and a spreading lower lip with darker markings near its base. Native from Europe to southwestern Siberia, it is introduced in North America, including British Columbia. Its nettle-like foliage can disguise its distinctive flowers until they open.

rumex-obtusifolius.summary: Broadleaf Dock is a sturdy perennial that starts as a rosette of large leaves with heart-shaped bases. Later it sends up a tall, ribbed flowering stem, with smaller leaves above and branching clusters of tiny greenish flowers. These clusters turn reddish brown as the fruits mature, and older foliage may also become reddish. A large fleshy taproot supports repeat growth. It is a familiar plant of disturbed ground and occurs along waterways in places such as Arizona.

sources.label: University of Missouri WeedID: Broadleaf dock

epipactis-helleborine.summary: Broadleaf helleborine is a terrestrial orchid with an upright stem, broad leaves and a loose line of small flowers. Its leaves alternate up the stem, with parallel veins and lower bases that partly wrap around it. Flowers combine green, pink or purplish tones and have a shaped lower lip rather than a long spur. Native across much of Europe and Asia and parts of North Africa, it has become established in North America, sometimes appearing in disturbed garden or woodland settings.

sources.label: University of Maryland Extension: Orchid in my garden

juncus-planifolius.summary: Broadleaf rush is a tufted perennial that can look like a small clump of grass until its branched flower clusters develop. Flat leaves gather at the base, while the stems carry an open, umbrella-like arrangement of small rounded flower heads. Brown capsules follow the flowers. It favors open, damp ground, including exposed clay and track or drain margins. Native in parts of the Southern Hemisphere, including New Zealand and Australia, it is introduced in places such as Hawaii and Oregon.

sources.label: New Zealand Plant Conservation Network: Juncus planifolius

lepidium-latifolium.summary: Broadleaved pepperweed is a tall perennial in the mustard family, with smooth green to gray-green leaves and dense sprays of tiny white flowers. New shoots begin as low rosettes before sending up stiff stems. Underground, an extensive root system stores energy and produces more shoots. Introduced from southeastern Europe and Asia, it forms persistent stands in parts of the western United States, especially around waterways, wetlands and irrigated ground. Seeds and root pieces can move it into new areas.

sources.label: UCSB Riparian InVasion Research Laboratory: Perennial pepperweed

vulpia-bromoides.summary: Brome fescue is a small annual grass with slender stems, narrow leaves and a compact, bristly flower cluster held clear of the uppermost leaf sheath. Its spikelets contain several flowers, each with a fine projecting awn. It grows in a wide range of open habitats, from coastal ground to dry inland sites, and is introduced from Europe in Washington. Some current references call it Festuca bromoides, while regional floras continue to use the catalog name Vulpia bromoides.

thaumastocoris-peregrinus.summary: Bronze bug is a tiny, flattened brown insect that lives on eucalyptus foliage. Adults and orange young insects may gather on the same leaves, alongside clusters of black eggs. Feeding can turn leaves reddish, then yellow-brown, giving affected crowns their bronze appearance; heavy infestations may thin the canopy. Native to Australia, it has spread to eucalyptus plantings in several other regions. Its small size and similarity to related bugs make a close examination more dependable than leaf discoloration alone.

sources.label: FAO: Bronze bug forest pest profile
Novoselsky and Freidberg: First record in the Middle East

odontites-vulgaris.summary: Odontites vulgaris, usually called red bartsia, is a downy annual of open grassland. Slender, branching stems carry narrow, toothed leaves and small pink flowers with two lips. Plants can reach about half a metre tall. They make their own green growth while also drawing resources from grass roots, a habit called partial parasitism. Native in Britain and Ireland, red bartsia also appears in Canadian floristic records. The catalog's name 'broomrape' should not obscure its leafy, green appearance.

anolis-sagrei.summary: Brown anoles are small, quick-moving lizards often seen basking on low fences, tree trunks and sunny garden edges. Their brown or gray bodies commonly show pale stripes, spots or diamonds, and males display an orange-red throat fan with a pale border. They hunt insects and other small animals, usually close to the ground. Native to Caribbean islands, they are widespread introductions in Florida. Native green anoles can also turn brown, so body color alone is not a reliable identification.

bugula-neritina.summary: Brown bryozoan forms branching, purplish-brown tufts that may look like miniature seaweed bushes. Each tuft is a colony of tiny animals that draw food particles from seawater. Colonies attach to rocks, pilings, floats, hulls and other submerged surfaces, sometimes becoming part of heavy marine fouling. The name Bugula neritina covers several genetically distinct forms with very similar appearances. Some have spread widely through human transport, while the origins and status of particular populations require closer investigation.

sources.label: Fehlauer-Ale et al.: Cryptic species in the Bugula neritina complex

cyperus-fuscus.summary: Brown flatsedge is a small annual sedge that forms tufts on damp, open ground beside ponds, streams and ditches. Smooth stems and narrow leaves support clusters of flattened flower spikes, often dark reddish-brown but sometimes yellow-green. It takes advantage of muddy or sandy margins exposed as water levels fall. The species is native across much of Europe and parts of Africa and Asia, with introduced records in North America. Its local status matters: in Germany, it is a native conservation concern.

sources.label: Kew Plants of the World Online: Cyperus fuscus

cornu-aspersum.summary: Brown garden snail carries a rounded, coiled shell patterned with brown bands and pale flecks. Adults are often about three centimetres across, although size and markings vary. Most feeding happens at night or in damp weather, when snails leave shelter to rasp leaves, flowers and soft fruit. Silvery trails can reveal visits after the animals have hidden again. Long transported with plants and for food, this European snail became a troublesome garden and crop pest in California after its nineteenth-century introduction.

sources.label: Dekle and Fasulo: Brown Garden Snail

hoplosternum-littorale.summary: Brown hoplo is a dark, armored catfish with two rows of hard plates along each side and two pairs of long whiskerlike barbels. It searches muddy bottoms for small invertebrates and decaying material in slow rivers, ponds, marshes and canals. Gulping air helps it cope with oxygen-poor water. Males make floating bubble nests mixed with vegetation and defend them during breeding. Native to South America, it has established in Florida, where its unusual nests have been documented in shallow lake marshes.

sources.label: Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission: Brown Hoplo
Nico and Muench: Nests and nest habitats of Hoplosternum littorale

halyomorpha-halys.summary: Brown marmorated stink bugs are broad, shield-shaped insects with mottled brown bodies and pale bands on their antennae. Adults are roughly the size of a fingernail. They feed on many fruits, vegetables and ornamental plants, and their feeding can leave fruit distorted or damaged. Native to eastern Asia, they have become important crop pests in parts of North America. In autumn, adults often gather on buildings while looking for winter shelter; finding them indoors does not mean they are breeding in the house.

sources.label: Penn State: Brown Marmorated Stink Bug
University of Maryland Extension: Brown Marmorated Stink Bug

brassica-juncea.summary: Brown mustard is a leafy mustard crop grown for pungent greens and seeds used in condiments and oil. Plants usually grow as annuals, producing clusters of yellow, four-petaled flowers followed by slender seed pods that split when dry. Leaves vary greatly among cultivated forms, from green to purple and from relatively smooth to deeply lobed. It grows best in cool weather with adequate moisture. Widely introduced beyond its Eurasian origins, it can also occur as a weed, so cultivated plants and wild escapes need different context.

sources.label: Kew Plants of the World Online: × Brassarda juncea

lyctus-brunneus.summary: Brown powderpost beetle is a small, flattened reddish-brown beetle associated with hardwood timber and wooden objects. Its cream-colored larvae tunnel through starch-rich sapwood, sometimes reducing the interior to very fine, flourlike powder. Round exit holes appear when adults emerge, making damage easier to notice than the insects themselves. Infested wood can carry the beetle between countries. The amount of damage depends on the wood and its sapwood content; powder and holes deserve identification before assumptions are made about structural danger.

sources.label: Natural History Museum: Lyctus brunneus identification

lecanosticta-acicola.summary: Lecanosticta acicola is a fungus that causes brown spot needle blight in pines. Small discolored spots can expand into brown bands, and infected needles may die at the tips or fall early, leaving a thin-looking crown. Wet needles and humid weather favor infection, while rain and wind spread spores. In New England, eastern white pine is a frequent host, though other pines are susceptible. Similar symptoms can come from other needle diseases, so the pattern of damage alone does not confirm this fungus.

sources.label: UMass Extension: Brown Spot Needle Blight
Scion: Brown spot needle blight factsheet

septoria-glycines.summary: Brown spot of soybean is a leaf disease caused by the fungus Septoria glycines. Small brown patches usually appear low on the plant, often surrounded by yellowing tissue. The patches can merge and affected leaves may fall early. Warm, wet weather helps the disease develop, while infected crop remains can carry the fungus into the next season. Brown spot is common in soybean fields and often has little effect on yield; more serious damage is possible when it moves into the upper canopy.

sources.label: NC State Extension: Brown spot of soybean

salmo-trutta.summary: Brown trout are introduced freshwater fish familiar to many anglers. Stream fish often have a golden-brown body with dark and reddish spots, while fish living in large lakes can look much more silvery. They eat aquatic insects and other small animals, including fish as they grow. Brought to the United States for fishing, they now live in many rivers and lakes. Their role depends on the waterway: some populations support managed fisheries, while others compete with native trout that conservation programs are working to protect.

sources.label: National Park Service: Yellowstone fish ecology

latrodectus-geometricus.summary: Brown widow spiders often make their webs in sheltered places around buildings, plant pots and outdoor furniture. Many are mottled tan or brown with an orange hourglass beneath the abdomen, but their colors vary enough to make identification tricky. Young black widows can look similar. A round egg sac covered in little silk spikes is a particularly useful clue. This nonnative spider is established in parts of the southern United States and Southern California. It can bite if pressed against the skin, so identification is best done without handling it.

sources.label: UC Riverside: How to identify brown widow spiders

niditinea-fuscella.summary: The brown-dotted clothes moth is a small, easily overlooked moth with mottled brown wings and a tufted head. Its larvae feed on dry plant and animal material, often in bird nests or poultry houses where feathers and other remains collect. Despite its name, it is only occasionally associated with damage to clothing. Stored animal specimens can also provide food. Adults resemble other small nest moths, so finding one indoors does not by itself show that fabrics are being damaged.

ruellia-blechum.summary: Browne's blechum is a low herb with paired leaves and upright flower spikes. The overlapping green bracts around those spikes are often more noticeable than the tiny pale flowers, giving the plant its other name, green shrimp plant. Its stems can spread along the ground and root where they touch the soil. Native to tropical parts of the Americas, it has become established beyond that range and is listed as invasive in Florida. The square-looking flower spikes are a useful starting point for recognizing it.

sources.label: University of South Florida FLIP: Ruellia blechum
Flora of China: Ruellia blechum via World Flora Online

centaurea-jacea.summary: Brown knapweed is a perennial wildflower with purple-pink flower heads on upright, branching stems. Beneath each head are overlapping bracts with broad, brown, papery tips that look unevenly torn. Native to Europe, it has become established in North America in fields, meadows and disturbed ground, and can form large patches. It also crosses with black knapweed, producing plants that blur the usual identification clues. A close look at the bracts is more useful than flower color alone.

euproctis-chrysorrhoea.summary: Browntail moths have white wings and a tuft of brown hair at the tip of the abdomen. Their caterpillars feed on trees and shrubs, including oaks, apples and cherries, and spend winter together in silk nests that hold dead leaves on branch tips. Established in parts of New England after introduction from Europe, they can strip foliage during outbreaks. The caterpillars' tiny hairs are also an important concern: they can irritate skin and breathing, even when carried on wind or left on surfaces.

watersipora-arcuata.summary: Watersipora arcuata is a marine animal that grows in colonies, often as dark crusts with reddish growing edges. A colony is made up of many tiny connected individuals and can develop overlapping, curled layers. It attaches to hard surfaces such as rocks, docks and boat hulls, which can carry it between harbors. Records from Southern California and Hawaii reflect its history of introductions, although its original native range remains uncertain. Similar Watersipora species are hard to separate without examining their tiny skeletal features.

sources.label: Reverter-Gil and Souto: Watersiporidae in Iberian waters

plantago-lanceolata.summary: Buckhorn plantain grows as a clump of narrow, strongly ribbed leaves close to the ground. Slender, leafless stalks rise above them, ending in short flower heads ringed with pale, projecting stamens. Originally from Eurasia, it is now a familiar plant in lawns, paths, fields and other disturbed places across much of North America. Its low-growing leaves help it persist under mowing. Compared with broadleaf plantain, the leaves are much narrower and the flowering heads are usually shorter and more compact.

aphis-nasturtii.summary: Buckthorn aphids are tiny, soft-bodied insects that feed on plant sap. They are usually pale yellow or green, and colonies can gather on the undersides of potato leaves. In colder regions they spend winter as eggs on buckthorn, then move to other plants during the growing season. Their importance in crops is not just the sap they take: they can carry potato viruses between plants. Several aphids look alike, making a careful identification useful before deciding how to respond.

sources.label: Government of New Brunswick: Buckthorn aphid
